obtained.how: NOAA Scientific Publications Office's own PDF of the article (Fishery Bulletin archive, fb42.8)

bibliography.checked_against: the article's first page and running heads
bibliography.corrections: entry is incomplete; it should read: Stewart, N. H. 1926. Development, growth, and food habits of the white sucker, Catostomus commersonii Lesueur. Bulletin of the U.S. Bureau of Fisheries 42: 147-184. (Author on the title page: Norman Hamilton Stewart; volume and pages match.)

claims.source_value: 54 °F (12.2 °C) is the water temperature at which, from 22 April, suckers were seen surfacing and leaping on the spawning ground; it is not given as an inlet reading or as the start of spawning. Ripe fish of both sexes were first trapped on 27 April in about 3 ft of water; the height of spawning was about 5 May and the season lasted about 29 days (to ~25 May, assumed). Stewart gives no 10 °C onset
claims.quote: Beginning April 22, whenever the water temperature reached 54° F. suckers were seen
claims.conditions: upper end of Beebee Lake, Ithaca, NY (a shallow artificial lake of about 6 acres), on the submerged gravel delta of the inflowing creek (a cool spring: air 5.6 °F below normal, 9 April-18 May)
claims.note: the surfacing habit's 'significance is uncertain' (Stewart). Write e.g. 'ripe fish from 27 April, spawning peak ~5 May at Beebee Lake; suckers active at the surface when the water reached 12.2 °C'. The '~10 °C' onset must come from another source in the row.

claims.quote: the inflowing creek spreads out over a delta of gravel and stones
claims.conditions: Beebee Lake's inlet delta, in water as shallow as about 1.5 ft; Stewart also saw a group spawn in a short stony rapid of Little Buffalo Creek, Union County, Pa., on 26 April 1925

claims.quote: The egg when laid measures 2 millimeters in diameter.
claims.conditions: swells to 3 mm total diameter within 30 minutes of water hardening

claims.claim: white sucker eggs are more than 90 % fertilized
claims.quote: Fertilization of well over 90 per cent of the eggs took place.
claims.conditions: artificial fertilization: eggs and sperm of one ripe pair (trapped 28 April) stripped into a dish at the Cornell University Fish-Cultural Experiment Station, stirred, water added after 3 minutes; not a field measurement
claims.note: §3.6.1 lists it beside field viability of perch ribbons; it should say 'in artificial (stripped) fertilization' so it is not read as a field rate (the research note egg_survival_and_larval_production.md already warns that the model once used it as hatch success)

claims.quote: probably 18 to 20 days is the normal period
claims.conditions: eggs in Meehan hatching jars supplied with the station's creek water; about 5 % hatched at 12 days, then a cold spell delayed hatching about a week, and all hatched in 2-3 days at 21 days; mean water temperature over the whole period 50.5 °F
claims.note: 50.5 °F = 10.3 °C (project conversion); 'The eggs in the Meehan jars hatched in 21 days' (same page)

claims.quote: Reighard (1915) gives 8 millimeters as the length of the newly hatched fry
claims.conditions: Stewart's own fry 'exceeded this by a millimeter or two, due, perhaps, to delayed hatching'
claims.note: the 8 mm is Reighard's (1915), as quoted by Stewart; Stewart's fry were about 9-10 mm

claims.location: p. 158 (PDF p. 14), Development of the larva (OCR garbled; read on the page image)
claims.quote: present for but six to eight days, when the larva is 11 millimeters
claims.conditions: hatchery larvae; the mouth opens at about 9 mm and food may be taken from 9 mm, though rarely

claims.claim: (Stewart 1926: ... no predation detected) [on white sucker eggs]
claims.note: Stewart says nothing about predation on sucker eggs. 'No predation on sucker eggs was detected' is Corbett & Powles 1986 (TAFS 115: 41, abstract), per the research note egg_stage.md; the comment should cite them.

notes: show.mjs listed no code lines for this key, but src/config.js:498 cites 'Stewart 1926: 21 d at 10.3 °C; > 90 % fertilised; no predation detected' (two of the three confirmed above). The 'fry drift at night ~1 month after spawning' and '16 d in a Jack Lake tributary' in the same table cell are Corbett & Powles 1983, not Stewart. Other values: spawners at Beebee Lake were 10-13 in long, though the species spawns at 6-7 in; 1-5 males pursue each female; Stewart estimated a 5-in sucker held 1,200 chironomids at once.
